This exercise follows [Calibrating Hedonic Pricing Model for Private Highrise
Property with GWR Method](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap13.html), the reading for the
Geographically Weighted Regression block of the course.

## 1. Overview

Everything up to Exercise 6 described where things are. This exercise asks a different
kind of question: **does the relationship between a price and its drivers stay the
same everywhere?**

An ordinary regression assumes it does. It fits one coefficient for floor area, one
for distance to the CBD, and applies them to a condominium in Bukit Timah and one in
Pasir Ris alike. That assumption is called spatial stationarity, and for housing it is
suspect on its face: an extra square metre is worth more where land is scarce, and
being close to an MRT station matters more where few people drive.

Geographically weighted regression (GWR) drops the assumption. It fits a separate
weighted regression at every observation, giving nearby observations more weight
through a kernel, so every coefficient becomes a surface rather than a number. The
cost is that every coefficient is now estimated from a small neighbourhood, and the
bandwidth that defines "small" becomes the most important decision in the model.

The application is a **hedonic pricing model**: price explained as the sum of what a
home offers, both structural (size, age, tenure) and locational (what it is near).

## 2. The Data

| Dataset | Description | Format |
|---|---|---|
| `MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL` | URA Master Plan 2014 subzone boundaries, 323 subzones | ESRI Shapefile (polygon) |
| `Condo_resale_2015.csv` | 1,436 condominium resale transactions in 2015, with structural and locational attributes | CSV, WGS 84 coordinates |

The condo file is the one distributed with the course. I checked my copy against three
independent student repositories, and all three are byte-identical to it.

## 3. Getting Started

```{r}
pacman::p_load(olsrr, corrplot, ggpubr,
               sf, sfdep, GWmodel, tmap,
               tidyverse, gtsummary,
               performance, see, RColorBrewer)
```

`see` is not in the handout's list, but `performance` needs it to draw its diagnostic
plots, so I load it explicitly rather than rely on it being installed already.

## 4. Geospatial Data Wrangling

### 4.1 Importing the subzone boundaries

```{r}
mpsz <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial",
                layer = "MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL")
```

The projection is SVY21, but `st_read()` cannot attach an EPSG code to it, which would
make every later transformation guess.

### 4.2 Updating the CRS

```{r}
mpsz_svy21 <- st_transform(mpsz, 3414)
st_crs(mpsz_svy21)$epsg
st_bbox(mpsz_svy21)
```

EPSG:3414 is SVY21 / Singapore TM, with metres as the unit. That unit matters later:
the fixed GWR bandwidth will be a distance in metres.

## 5. Aspatial Data Wrangling

### 5.1 Importing the transactions

```{r}
condo_resale <- read_csv("data/aspatial/Condo_resale_2015.csv")
glimpse(condo_resale)
```

```{r}
summary(condo_resale$SELLING_PRICE)
```

The median price is S$1.38 million and the maximum S$18 million, thirteen times the
median. A distribution with that tail will shape every least-squares fit below.

### 5.2 Converting to an sf object

```{r}
condo_resale.sf <- st_as_sf(condo_resale,
                            coords = c("LONGITUDE", "LATITUDE"),
                            crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)
head(condo_resale.sf, 3)
```

The coordinates are longitude and latitude, so they are declared as WGS 84 (4326) and
then projected to SVY21 to match the subzones.

## 6. Exploratory Data Analysis

### 6.1 The selling price

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3
p1 <- ggplot(condo_resale.sf, aes(x = SELLING_PRICE)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "black", fill = "light blue") +
  labs(title = "SELLING_PRICE")

condo_resale.sf <- condo_resale.sf %>%
  mutate(LOG_SELLING_PRICE = log(SELLING_PRICE))

p2 <- ggplot(condo_resale.sf, aes(x = LOG_SELLING_PRICE)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "black", fill = "light blue") +
  labs(title = "log(SELLING_PRICE)")

ggarrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2)
```

The raw price is strongly right-skewed; the log is close to symmetric. The handout
derives the log and then models the raw price anyway. I follow it, because the point
of the exercise is GWR rather than the best hedonic specification, but I return to
the consequence in section 11.

### 6.2 The independent variables

```{r}
#| fig-height: 7
vars <- c("AREA_SQM", "AGE", "PROX_CBD", "PROX_CHILDCARE",
          "PROX_ELDERLYCARE", "PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA",
          "PROX_HAWKER_MARKET", "PROX_KINDERGARTEN", "PROX_MRT",
          "PROX_PARK", "PROX_PRIMARY_SCH", "PROX_TOP_PRIMARY_SCH")

hists <- lapply(vars, function(v) {
  ggplot(condo_resale.sf, aes(x = .data[[v]])) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 20, color = "black", fill = "light blue") +
    labs(x = v, y = NULL) +
    theme(axis.title.x = element_text(size = 8))
})
ggarrange(plotlist = hists, ncol = 3, nrow = 4)
```

The handout builds these twelve histograms one assignment at a time. I build them in
a loop over the variable names: same plots, and adding a variable is one word. Most
proximity variables are right-skewed, as distances usually are: most condos are near
a childcare centre or a bus stop and a few are far from everything.

### 6.3 Where the prices are

```{r}
tmap_mode("plot")
tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey75", lwd = 0.3) +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf) +
  tm_dots(fill = "SELLING_PRICE",
          fill_alpha = 0.7,
          size = 0.25,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                          values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Selling price (S$)")) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)
```

The handout draws this as an interactive map. I draw it static so the page stays light,
and keep one interactive map for section 9.5 where zooming genuinely helps. The
pattern is clear without zooming: the most expensive class is almost entirely in the
Central Region. Joining the points to URA regions, 40% of Central Region transactions
fall in the top price quintile, against 5% or less in every other region.

## 7. Hedonic Pricing with Ordinary Least Squares

### 7.1 Simple linear regression

```{r}
condo.slr <- lm(SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM, data = condo_resale.sf)
summary(condo.slr)
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.5
ggplot(condo_resale.sf, aes(x = AREA_SQM, y = SELLING_PRICE)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = lm)
```

Floor area alone explains 45% of the variance in price. Each extra square metre adds
about S$14,700. The scatterplot shows why the fit is not better: a band of very
expensive units sits far above the line at every size, which is location speaking.

### 7.2 Checking for multicollinearity

```{r}
#| fig-height: 7
corrplot(cor(condo_resale[, 5:23]),
         diag = FALSE,
         order = "AOE",
         tl.pos = "td",
         tl.cex = 0.5,
         method = "number",
         type = "upper")
```

`FREEHOLD` and `LEASEHOLD_99YR` are strongly negatively correlated, which is close to
true by definition: a unit that is not freehold is almost always on a 99-year lease.
Keeping both would make their coefficients unstable, so `LEASEHOLD_99YR` is dropped.

### 7.3 The full multiple regression

```{r}
condo.mlr <- lm(SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE +
                  PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
                  PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_HAWKER_MARKET +
                  PROX_KINDERGARTEN + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
                  PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_TOP_PRIMARY_SCH +
                  PROX_SHOPPING_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET +
                  PROX_BUS_STOP + NO_Of_UNITS +
                  FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD,
                data = condo_resale.sf)
summary(condo.mlr)
```

Four variables are not significant at 5%: `PROX_HAWKER_MARKET`, `PROX_KINDERGARTEN`,
`PROX_TOP_PRIMARY_SCH` and `PROX_SUPERMARKET`.

### 7.4 The revised model

```{r}
condo.mlr1 <- lm(SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE +
                   PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_MRT +
                   PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA +
                   PROX_PARK + PROX_PRIMARY_SCH +
                   PROX_SHOPPING_MALL + PROX_BUS_STOP +
                   NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD,
                 data = condo_resale.sf)

tbl_regression(condo.mlr1, intercept = TRUE) %>%
  add_glance_source_note(
    label = list(sigma ~ "\U03C3"),
    include = c(r.squared, adj.r.squared,
                AIC, statistic, p.value, sigma))
```

Dropping the four costs almost nothing: adjusted R² moves from 0.6474 to 0.6472. Every
remaining predictor is significant. Some signs are worth a second look rather than a
nod. `PROX_PRIMARY_SCH` and `PROX_PARK` have positive coefficients, so price *rises*
with distance from a primary school or a park, which runs against the family-buyer
story. More likely those facilities are densest in the cheaper outer estates, while
the most expensive condos sit in central districts with fewer of them. That is the
first hint that one coefficient for the whole island is averaging over different
markets.

### 7.5 Regression diagnostics

#### Multicollinearity

```{r}
check_collinearity(condo.mlr1)
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
plot(check_collinearity(condo.mlr1))
```

Every VIF is below 3.3, far from the conventional warning level of 5 or 10. Globally,
collinearity is not a problem. Section 11.2 shows why that reassurance does not carry
over to GWR.

#### Linearity

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
check_model(condo.mlr1, check = "linearity")
```

The residuals are centred on zero across most of the fitted range, with a fan at the
expensive end. Linearity is acceptable; constant variance is not.

#### Normality of residuals

```{r}
check_normality(condo.mlr1)
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4
check_model(condo.mlr1, check = "normality")
```

The Shapiro-Wilk test rejects normality decisively. The handout reads the density plot
as roughly normal, and it is in the middle. The tails are not: the Q-Q plot bends away
at both ends, the signature of the long upper tail from section 6.1.

### 7.6 Spatial autocorrelation in the residuals

This is the test that motivates GWR. If the model has captured everything that
matters, its errors should be spatially random. If location still matters, residuals
will cluster.

```{r}
condo_resale.sf <- cbind(condo_resale.sf,
                         condo.mlr1$residuals) %>%
  rename(MLR_RES = condo.mlr1.residuals)
```

```{r}
tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey75", lwd = 0.3) +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf) +
  tm_dots(fill = "MLR_RES",
          size = 0.25,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            n = 10, style = "quantile",
            values = rev(brewer.pal(11, "RdBu"))),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "OLS residual")) +
  tm_title("OLS residuals (quantile classes)") +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE, legend.outside = TRUE)
```

Red points are under-predicted (they sold for more than the model says), blue
over-predicted. They are not scattered at random. Counting by URA region, 80% of
North Region residuals are positive and 68% of North-East Region residuals are
negative: the global model systematically under-prices one area and over-prices
another.

```{r}
condo_resale.sf <- condo_resale.sf %>%
  mutate(nb = st_dist_band(st_geometry(geometry), upper = 1500),
         wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"),
         .before = 1)

set.seed(1234)
global_moran_perm(condo_resale.sf$MLR_RES,
                  nb = condo_resale.sf$nb,
                  wt = condo_resale.sf$wt,
                  alternative = "two.sided",
                  nsim = 499)
```

Moran's I is 0.144 with every one of 499 permutations below it. The residuals are
clustered. The global model has left location-specific structure in its errors, which
is exactly the condition GWR is designed for.

## 8. A Short Note on GWmodel

`GWmodel` provides a family of geographically weighted methods: summary statistics,
principal components, discriminant analysis, and several forms of GWR (basic, robust,
generalised, mixed, and multiscale). This exercise uses the basic form, `gwr.basic()`,
with its bandwidth selector `bw.gwr()`.

## 9. Geographically Weighted Regression

The bandwidth decides how many observations each local regression sees. Too wide and
GWR collapses back to the global model; too narrow and each local fit is estimated
from a handful of points and chases noise. `bw.gwr()` chooses it by cross-validation:
leave each observation out, predict it from its neighbours, and pick the bandwidth
that minimises the squared prediction error.

There are two ways to define "neighbourhood". A **fixed** bandwidth uses the same
distance everywhere. An **adaptive** bandwidth uses the same *number* of neighbours
everywhere, so the radius stretches where condos are sparse and shrinks where they
are dense.

### 9.1 Fixed bandwidth

```{r}
#| results: hide
bw.fixed <- bw.gwr(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL +
    PROX_BUS_STOP + NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY +
    FREEHOLD,
  data = condo_resale.sf,
  approach = "CV",
  kernel = "gaussian",
  adaptive = FALSE,
  longlat = FALSE)
```

```{r}
bw.fixed
```

I hide the cross-validation trace, which prints dozens of lines of CV scores. The
chosen bandwidth is about 971 m. My run lands on 971.34 m, which matches the handout's
text; the handout's printed output shows 971.39 m. The difference is the stopping
tolerance of the golden-section search, half a metre either way, and has no effect on
anything below.

```{r}
gwr.fixed <- gwr.basic(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL +
    PROX_BUS_STOP + NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY +
    FREEHOLD,
  data = condo_resale.sf,
  bw = bw.fixed,
  kernel = "gaussian",
  longlat = FALSE)
gwr.fixed
```

### 9.2 Adaptive bandwidth

```{r}
#| results: hide
bw.adaptive <- bw.gwr(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL +
    PROX_BUS_STOP + NO_Of_UNITS +
    FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD,
  data = condo_resale.sf,
  approach = "CV",
  kernel = "gaussian",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  longlat = FALSE)
```

```{r}
bw.adaptive
```

```{r}
gwr.adaptive <- gwr.basic(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
    PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL + PROX_BUS_STOP +
    NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD,
  data = condo_resale.sf,
  bw = bw.adaptive,
  kernel = "gaussian",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  longlat = FALSE)
gwr.adaptive
```

### 9.3 Comparing the three models

```{r}
tibble(
  model = c("OLS (global)", "GWR, fixed bandwidth", "GWR, adaptive bandwidth"),
  bandwidth = c("-", paste(round(bw.fixed), "m"), paste(bw.adaptive, "neighbours")),
  # AICc for OLS: AIC plus the small-sample correction, with k = 16
  # (15 coefficients and the residual variance)
  AICc = c(AIC(condo.mlr1) + 2 * 16 * 17 / (nrow(condo_resale.sf) - 16 - 1),
           gwr.fixed$GW.diagnostic$AICc, gwr.adaptive$GW.diagnostic$AICc),
  adj_R2 = c(summary(condo.mlr1)$adj.r.squared,
             gwr.fixed$GW.diagnostic$gwR2.adj, gwr.adaptive$GW.diagnostic$gwR2.adj),
  effective_parameters = c(15, gwr.fixed$GW.diagnostic$enp, gwr.adaptive$GW.diagnostic$enp)
) %>% mutate(across(c(AICc, adj_R2, effective_parameters), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

Both GWR models improve on the global model by a wide margin: AICc falls by about 700
(fixed) and 985 (adaptive), and adjusted R² rises from 0.65 to 0.84 and 0.86. AICc
penalises the extra effective parameters, so this is not just a more flexible model
fitting better; it is a better model after paying for the flexibility.

The adaptive model wins on every measure and uses fewer effective parameters (350
against 438). That makes sense for Singapore condos, which are dense in the centre and
sparse at the edges: a fixed 971 m window holds dozens of transactions in the core and
only a few on the periphery, while 30 neighbours gives every local fit the same amount
of evidence.

### 9.4 Converting the output to sf

```{r}
condo_resale.sf.adaptive <- st_as_sf(gwr.adaptive$SDF) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)
summary(gwr.adaptive$SDF$yhat)
```

The `SDF` holds, for every transaction, its local coefficients, their standard errors
and t-values, the fitted value, the residual and a local R².

### 9.5 Local R²

```{r}
tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
  tm_polygons(fill_alpha = 0.1) +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf.adaptive) +
  tm_dots(fill = "Local_R2",
          size = 0.15,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                          values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(11, 14))
tmap_mode("plot")
```

```{r}
summary(condo_resale.sf.adaptive$Local_R2)
```

Local R² runs from 0.67 to 0.99, with a median of 0.91. The local models are weakest
on the fringe of the central area, in Bishan, Toa Payoh, Bukit Merah and Novena
(medians 0.73 to 0.82), where prime and mass-market condos sit within the same
30-neighbour window. They are strongest in the North Region (median 0.99), where the
market is more uniform.

### 9.6 Mapping a coefficient: floor area

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.5
AREA_SQM_SE <- tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey80", lwd = 0.2) +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf.adaptive) +
  tm_dots(fill = "AREA_SQM_SE", size = 0.15,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", values = "brewer.purples"),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Std. error")) +
  tm_title("Standard error of AREA_SQM") +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)

AREA_SQM_TV <- tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey80", lwd = 0.2) +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf.adaptive) +
  tm_dots(fill = "AREA_SQM_TV", size = 0.15,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", values = "brewer.purples"),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "t-value")) +
  tm_title("t-value of AREA_SQM") +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)

tmap_arrange(AREA_SQM_SE, AREA_SQM_TV, ncol = 2)
```

The handout maps the standard error and the t-value, but not the coefficient itself,
which is the thing GWR exists to produce. I add it:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.5
tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey80", lwd = 0.2) +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf.adaptive) +
  tm_dots(fill = "AREA_SQM", size = 0.2,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "S$ per sq m")) +
  tm_title("Local coefficient of AREA_SQM") +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE, legend.outside = TRUE)
```

```{r}
range(condo_resale.sf.adaptive$AREA_SQM)
coef(condo.mlr1)["AREA_SQM"]
```

This is the result the whole exercise has been building towards. The global model
says an extra square metre adds S$12,800 everywhere. GWR says it adds between about
S$3,300 and S$23,000 depending on where the condo is, a sevenfold range, and the
highest values are in the prime central districts: the median local coefficient is
about S$18,900 in Newton, S$16,800 in Novena and S$16,400 in Tanglin, against roughly
S$5,300 to S$7,000 in the East, North, North-East and West regions. The global coefficient is an
average over markets that price space very differently.

## 10. Do the Local Models Fix the Residuals?

Section 7.6 established that the global model's residuals cluster. The natural test of
GWR is to run the same test on its residuals, with the same weights and seed. The
handout stops before doing this.

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
global_moran_perm(condo_resale.sf.adaptive$residual,
                  nb = condo_resale.sf$nb,
                  wt = condo_resale.sf$wt,
                  alternative = "two.sided",
                  nsim = 499)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## GWR removes the clustering, and slightly overshoots

Moran's I on the residuals falls from **+0.144** under OLS to **−0.016** under adaptive
GWR. The positive clustering is gone. What remains is small and *negative*, and at
p = 0.024 it is still distinguishable from zero.

A negative residual autocorrelation means neighbouring condos now tend to have errors
of opposite sign. With a 30-neighbour kernel, each local fit is pulled hard towards
its own neighbourhood, so it slightly over-explains local variation. That is a mild
symptom of the bandwidth being on the small side, consistent with the 350 effective
parameters for 1,436 observations. It is not a reason to reject the model, but it is
a reason not to read the very highest local R² values as pure signal.
:::

## 11. Two Things the Handout's Diagnostics Do Not Catch

### 11.1 How many local coefficients are actually significant?

```{r}
tv <- condo_resale.sf.adaptive %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(ends_with("_TV"), -Intercept_TV)

tibble(variable = sub("_TV$", "", names(tv)),
       share_significant = round(colMeans(abs(tv) > 1.96), 2)) %>%
  arrange(desc(share_significant))
```

In the global model every one of these fourteen predictors was significant. Locally,
only floor area is significant almost everywhere (96% of locations). Most locational
variables are significant at fewer than a third of locations. So the global result
"proximity to a park matters" is better read as "proximity to a park matters in some
neighbourhoods", which is more useful and less tidy.

One caution on the column above: it applies an unadjusted |t| > 1.96 at 1,436
overlapping locations, so it overstates significance rather than understates it.
Corrections designed for GWR (da Silva and Fotheringham, 2016) would shrink these
shares further.

### 11.2 Local collinearity

Section 7.5 found no collinearity problem in the global model: every VIF below 3.3.
That check was done on the whole island. GWR does not fit on the whole island; it fits
on 30 neighbours at a time, and variables that are independent across Singapore can be
nearly redundant inside one neighbourhood. `GWmodel` provides a local diagnostic.

```{r}
xvars <- c("AREA_SQM", "AGE", "PROX_CBD", "PROX_CHILDCARE",
           "PROX_ELDERLYCARE", "PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA", "PROX_MRT",
           "PROX_PARK", "PROX_PRIMARY_SCH", "PROX_SHOPPING_MALL",
           "PROX_BUS_STOP", "NO_Of_UNITS", "FAMILY_FRIENDLY", "FREEHOLD")

# Condition numbers depend on the units of the variables, so standardise
# first; otherwise NO_Of_UNITS (hundreds) against distances (km) would
# inflate the number for reasons that have nothing to do with collinearity.
condo_z <- condo_resale.sf %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(xvars), ~ as.numeric(scale(.x))))

collin <- gwr.collin.diagno(
  formula = SELLING_PRICE ~ AREA_SQM + AGE + PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE +
    PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_PRIMARY_SCH + PROX_SHOPPING_MALL + PROX_BUS_STOP +
    NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD,
  data = condo_z,
  bw = bw.adaptive,
  kernel = "gaussian",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  longlat = FALSE)

local_cn <- collin$SDF$local_CN
c(over_30 = sum(local_cn > 30), n = length(local_cn),
  median = round(median(local_cn), 1))
```

```{r}
local_vif <- st_drop_geometry(st_as_sf(collin$SDF)) %>% select(ends_with("_VIF"))
tibble(variable = sub("_VIF$", "", names(local_vif)),
       median_local_VIF = round(apply(local_vif, 2, median), 1),
       share_over_10 = round(colMeans(local_vif > 10), 2)) %>%
  arrange(desc(share_over_10)) %>%
  head(6)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## The global model was clean; the local models are not

Even after standardising, the local condition number exceeds 30, the usual warning
level, at **`r sum(local_cn > 30)` of `r length(local_cn)`** locations, with a median of
**`r round(median(local_cn))`**. For comparison, the condition number of the global
design matrix is about 4.

The local VIFs say where it comes from. `PROX_CBD` has a local VIF above 10 in more
than half of all neighbourhoods, and `PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA` in about half. The reason
is geometric. Across the whole island, distance to the CBD and distance to a growth
area vary independently enough. Inside a cluster of 30 nearby condos, both are close
to smooth linear functions of the same two coordinates, so the local regression
cannot tell them apart.

The practical consequence is that the local coefficient maps for `PROX_CBD` and
`PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA` should not be interpreted one at a time: their surfaces trade
off against each other. The floor-area surface in section 9.6 is safe; its local VIF
never exceeds 10. This is the kind of problem the handout's single global VIF check
cannot see, and it is the reason the GWR literature recommends local diagnostics
(Wheeler and Tiefelsdorf, 2005) or a multiscale GWR that lets each variable choose its
own bandwidth.
:::

## 12. What I Take From This Exercise

**Stationarity is an assumption you can test, and here it fails.** The OLS residuals
cluster (Moran's I 0.144), GWR removes that clustering, and AICc falls by almost a
thousand after paying for the extra parameters. For condo prices in Singapore, one
coefficient per variable is the wrong model.

**The coefficient surface is the result.** The handout maps the standard error and
t-value of floor area; the map that matters is the coefficient itself, which runs from
about S$3,300 to S$23,000 per square metre across the island against a single global
S$12,800. That spread is the thing a valuer or a developer would actually use.

**The adaptive bandwidth is not just a better fit, it is the right shape for the
data.** Condos are dense in the centre and sparse at the edge. A fixed radius gives
some local regressions far more evidence than others; a fixed neighbour count does
not. It wins on AICc with fewer effective parameters.

**A clean global diagnostic does not certify a local model.** This is the finding I
will carry forward. Every VIF in the global model was under 3.3, and yet most local
regressions are badly conditioned, because variables that are distinct across a
country become near-duplicates within a neighbourhood. Local coefficients for
location variables that are themselves smooth functions of position need local
diagnostics before anyone reads them.

**What I would change.** Model log price rather than price, since section 6.1 showed
the raw price has a thirteen-fold tail that dominates least squares, and try a
multiscale GWR so that floor area, which seems to vary at a district scale, is not
forced to share a 30-neighbour bandwidth with the proximity variables.
